channel.title: the vfx supervisor
channel.description: Notes on VFX supervision, breakdowns, budgets and pipeline.

item.title: My agent sold my old furniture and saved me more than 50 hours
item.description: Ten days of listing, pricing and replying across two marketplaces, handed to an AI agent while I did everything else: 96 listings, about 290 buyer messages, more than 50 hours saved. What it was good at, what it still needed me for, and the traps marketplace sites set for automation.

item.title: A clean licence is not clean provenance
item.description: Every model file in a generative pipeline matched its publisher by hash, and all but one were permissively licensed. That answers whether you may use the weights. It does not answer what a client actually asks.

item.title: Pin the deliverable, not the recipe
item.description: Re-running an approved generative shot does not reliably give it back, and raising the resolution quietly re-frames it. Why the approved file is the asset, not the settings.

item.title: The ControlNet that was not broken
item.description: A depth control that did nothing on one model worked strongly on its sibling. Why model family is not a detail, and why a test only means something when the signals disagree.

item.title: Every gate is a person, and that is the product
item.description: A generative video pipeline where the tracker is the state machine, a deterministic check can only refuse, and nothing ever self-approves. Drawn.

item.title: Config in, coordination out: the shape of an agent fleet
item.description: Two separate paths carry a rulebook into an AI agent's session, and confusing them is the mistake. What a working multi-agent fleet looks like, drawn.

item.title: The negative prompt that does nothing
item.description: On a speed-LoRA recipe at guidance 1.0, the negative prompt is never read. Measured four ways, traced to one line of the sampler, and why it changed how every instruction was written.

item.title: The cheapest message is the one nobody sends
item.description: A fleet of AI agents coordinating on the same work gets noisy fast, and the noise is billed. Why the fix is a systems change, not better instructions.

item.title: The eleven things I check
item.description: A post producer asked how you know a VFX shot looks real. Real is the wrong test. The tells a supervisor checks, from black point to lens characteristics.

item.title: The bad monitor
item.description: A supervisor on Eastwood films learned a trick at ILM: check the finished shot on the worst screen in the building. Why comparison beats memory.

item.title: How a one-person VFX department orchestrates AI
item.description: The mechanical half automates. The judgment half stays with the supervisor. Notes on briefing an AI assistant with guardrails on a live production.

item.title: Running several AI agents as one coordinated team
item.description: A shared folder and a few JSON files let a fleet of AI agents work one production: handing off work, staying out of each other's way, across restarts.

item.title: Keeping a long-running AI agent in sync with its own rules
item.description: An AI agent that runs for days works from the rulebook it read on day one. Updating it without restarting or drowning it: notify always, load on demand.
